picks.style: greek consolation ode, lyre and low strings, grave tenor, slow, measured, autumnal
picks.why: The leaves simile — 'Another race the following spring supplies; they fall successive, and successive rise' — the oldest image we have for mortality.

picks.style: dark chamber ballad, viol and muted harp, low female voice, slow, hushed, creeping
picks.why: Pandora's plagues creeping on silent feet because Jupiter took away their voices — a nightmare with a beautiful mechanism.

picks.style: ancient greek gnomic chant, single lyre and drone, plain male voice, unhurried, aphoristic, sparse
picks.why: 'What are we, what are we not? Man is but a shadow's dream' — Pindar's hyperbole set against a wheel that turns in a single day.

picks.style: roman stage aria, tibia pipes and light strings, warm female voice, flowing, resigned, dignified
picks.why: Alcmena alone: pleasure allotted sorrow for a companion, one night of a husband, and valour named the best reward — a real solo speech.

picks.style: comic patter song, plucked lyre and hand drum, sly light tenor, quick, conspiratorial, mischievous
picks.why: Mercury planning to fake a drunk and pelt a man from his own rooftop — a self-contained aside told straight to the audience.

picks.style: roman market-god prologue, reedy pipes and tambourine, brash showman's voice, brisk, wheedling, rhythmic
picks.why: The god of profit bargaining with the crowd for their silence before naming himself — a prologue that is already a performance.

picks.style: english supernatural ballad, fiddle and harp, plaintive female voice, strophic, ominous, unhurried
picks.why: Colin and Lucy — the bell tolling three times and the raven at the window. Ballad metre with a curse in it.

picks.style: georgian elegy-hymn, chamber organ and strings, clear tenor, slow, questioning, ascending
picks.why: 'In what new region, to the just assign'd, what new employments please th' unbody'd mind?' — a whole song of questions to the dead.

picks.style: solemn valediction, muted strings and low flute, grave baritone, slow, bitter, spare
picks.why: 'Thou musick, warbling to the deafen'd ear! Thou incense wasted on the fun'ral bier!' — fame indicted in four unanswerable lines.

picks.style: english dance-song, tabor and pipe with fiddle, bright female voice, quick, whirling, refrain-driven
picks.why: 'Come, let us dance and sing' — short lines, internal rhyme, a built-in chorus. It is already a song and says so.

picks.style: dawn aubade, harp and soft flute, high clear voice, gathering, expectant, luminous
picks.why: The poet of spring calling the hours on: 'Swift, swift, ye lingering hours, and wake the morning star.'

picks.style: pastoral chase ballad, acoustic guitar and fiddle, warm mixed voices, lilting, teasing, seasonal
picks.why: The girl who laughs and runs across three seasons of hills — a pursuit song with the year built into its verses.

picks.style: witty georgian air, harpsichord and recorder, light tenor, tripping, charming, four-beat
picks.why: The oak dropping acorns down your neck, birds taking their vacation to sing, flowers leaning out to trade sweets — invention on every line.

picks.style: reflective english hymn, chamber organ and viola, calm baritone, slow, settled, consoling
picks.why: 'A stranger into life I'm come, dying may be our going home' — the whole argument for peace of mind in twelve lines.

picks.style: drawing-room lament, harpsichord and solo violin, tender soprano, gentle, reproachful, strophic
picks.why: The sparrow killed to mend a ring, closing on 'A Lucia's face forbear to smile, a Venus kill her bird.'

picks.style: greek tragic monody, aulos and low lyre, resolute female voice, measured, unwavering, austere
picks.why: The mother giving her daughter to be sacrificed, scorning the women who urge cowardice — a garland destined for her alone.

picks.style: spartan war chant, deep drum and bronze percussion, massed male voices, hard, driving, stamping
picks.why: Tyrtaeus at full pitch, closing on the greatest epitaph ever cut: 'Go tell the Spartans ... that here obedient to their laws we lie.'

picks.style: greek marching song, double pipe and frame drum, low male chorus, insistent, grim, steady
picks.why: The exile roaming unpitied with his whole line behind him, turned into a reason to stand and guard the old.

picks.style: homeric recitation, single lyre and low drone, declaiming male voice, deliberate, ominous, spare
picks.why: The eagle and the still-fighting snake that bites its captor and is dropped into the army — a complete omen in one breath.
